opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important and hardest measurement questions right now. There are a few layers to it.

The most common approach is benchmarks: can the model solve SWE-bench tasks, or how long a task, measured in human-expert time, can it complete autonomously at some reliability threshold? Those are really valuable, and the trend lines have been striking. But they measure capability in a controlled setting, not whether the work of building software or doing AI research is actually happening faster. Those two things can come apart a lot.

So the second layer is field measurement: randomized controlled trials where you give developers AI tools on some tasks and not others, and measure how long things take. What's humbling about those studies is that developers' self-reports can diverge sharply from measured outcomes. People feel much faster even when the measured effect is small or sometimes negative, at least on large, mature codebases where the developer has deep context. That tells me we shouldn't rely on vibes or surveys, including from people inside AI companies, who are often the most enthusiastic users.

The third layer, and the one I care most about, is uplift on AI R&D specifically, because that's where you could get a feedback loop: AI making AI research faster, which makes better AI, and so on. There I'd want companies to track things like how much of their research engineering is being done by AI agents, how fast experiments go from idea to result, and the rate of algorithmic progress, meaning how much compute it takes to reach a given capability level over time. If that efficiency curve starts bending upward faster than the historical trend, that's a real signal.

Ideally you'd have something like a standing internal RCT, or at least careful before-and-after productivity tracking, plus disclosure to some outside party. I don't think it's reasonable to expect the public to see everything, but I'd love it if labs committed to measuring this rigorously and sharing it with governments or third-party evaluators. If we get to a world where most AI research is done by AI systems, I don't want us to find out from a press release after the fact. We want early warning, and we want measures that are hard to fool ourselves with.

r001.rationale: It proposes randomized controlled trials giving developers AI tools on some tasks and not others, then measuring task duration.

r002.rationale: It says measured effects can be small or sometimes negative on mature codebases, but does not identify the METR trial or clearly report that AI slowed task completion in that trial.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes benchmark capability from actual development speed and recommends field measurement to assess whether work is happening faster.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, and I think the honest answer is that there's no single clean metric, and most of the things people reach for first are pretty misleading.

The thing people most often cite is some version of "X percent of our code is now written by AI." I think that's close to useless as a measure of speedup. The fraction of characters that come out of a model tells you almost nothing about whether the humans in the loop are getting more done per unit time. You can have a world where ninety percent of the tokens are AI-generated and the engineer is spending all their time reviewing and fixing those tokens, and you've gained maybe ten or twenty percent. So I'd set that one aside.

The second thing people point to is self-report. Surveys of engineers saying "I feel like I'm twice as fast." I take those seriously as a signal, but we have pretty good evidence now that people are not great at estimating this. The METR uplift study from last year is the one I keep coming back to, where experienced open-source developers predicted they'd be sped up by something like twenty-plus percent and the measured effect was actually a slowdown. That result has been argued about a lot, and I don't think it generalizes to every setting, but it should make you skeptical of vibes-based estimates in either direction.

So what would I actually want? I'd break it into a few layers.

The first is randomized controlled uplift studies, like the METR one, but more of them, across more task types and more skill levels, and repeated over time as the models improve. The thing I'd want to see is not just one number but a trajectory. If the measured uplift on realistic, multi-hour tasks is going from negative to small positive to large positive over successive model generations, that's the most direct evidence you can get.

The second layer is what I'd call the "horizon length" style measures. How long of a task, measured in the time it would take a competent human, can the model complete autonomously at some reliability threshold. That's less about speedup per se and more about what fraction of the work is becoming fully delegable. And I think that's actually the quantity that matters most for the AI R&D question specifically, because the scary dynamic isn't "humans are thirty percent faster," it's "whole chunks of the research loop no longer need a human at all."

The third layer, and this is the hardest, is looking at the labs themselves. If AI is genuinely accelerating AI research, you'd expect to see it in things like the rate of experiments run per researcher, the time from idea to result, or the number of researchers needed to ship a given capability. Those numbers mostly aren't public, and even internally they're confounded by compute growth and headcount growth. But I think the labs should be tracking this carefully, and I'd love to see some of them publish even coarse versions of it, because it's the actual thing we're worried about.

And then there's a caveat I'd put on all of this, which is that measuring the easy-to-measure parts can fool you. Writing a function is easy to benchmark. Deciding what the right experiment is, noticing that your results are confounded, having the taste to know which direction is worth pursuing, those are the parts of R&D that take the most senior people the most time, and we have very few good measures of whether AI is helping there yet. My guess is that's where the real bottleneck sits for a while, and it's also where the transition, when it happens, would be most consequential.

So if someone asks me for one number, I'd say: measured uplift on long, realistic tasks in a controlled setting, tracked over time. But I'd want to say it with the caveat that the number you can measure well isn't necessarily the one that matters most.

r001.rationale: It proposes more randomized controlled uplift studies across task types and skill levels, which clearly conveys comparing performance with and without AI.

r002.rationale: It says the METR study found the measured effect was a slowdown, despite developers predicting a speedup.

r003.rationale: It discusses controlled task studies and lab productivity measures, but does not explicitly advocate cross-checking benchmark evaluations against evidence of workplace speedups.

astra-6.text:
I’d want to distinguish between making a particular task faster and making the whole process faster. You might find that someone can write a piece of code much more quickly with AI, but that doesn’t necessarily mean they can ship a useful product much more quickly. They still have to decide what to build, check that it works, integrate it, and maintain it.

So ideally, you’d compare teams with and without access to AI on substantial projects, and ask how long it takes them to reach the same standard of quality. You’d want to include the time spent reviewing and fixing the AI’s work. And you’d want to give people enough time to learn how to use the tools, because handing someone a tool for an afternoon doesn’t tell you what a team that reorganizes around it can accomplish.

For AI R&D, I think the distinction is even more important. Running more experiments isn’t necessarily the same as making more progress. The question is whether you’re getting better research results, with a fixed amount of compute and human effort, or reaching a given result sooner.

And then I’d be especially interested in where the bottlenecks move. If implementing an experiment becomes very cheap, does choosing the right experiment become the constraint? Can AI help interpret the results and decide what to try next? That tells you much more about the potential for further acceleration than a measurement of coding speed alone.

r001.rationale: It proposes comparing teams with and without AI on substantial projects, but does not specify randomized trials.

r002.rationale: It does not report that AI access slowed task completion in the METR trial.

r003.rationale: It discusses measuring project outcomes and quality, but does not advocate cross-checking benchmark evaluations against workplace speedup evidence.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d want to distinguish between making a particular task faster and speeding up the whole process. You can have an AI that writes code much faster, but if people spend more time reviewing it, or if writing code wasn’t the main bottleneck, that might not translate into a big increase in productivity.

So, for software development, I’d ideally look at how long it takes to deliver a working feature, at a given level of quality, with and without AI. And I’d want to measure that over a reasonably long period, so you capture things like bugs and maintenance costs, rather than just whether someone finished a coding exercise faster.

AI R&D is harder, because the output you care about is research progress. Running more experiments isn’t necessarily progress if those experiments aren’t very informative. I’d want to look at whether teams can reach a given capability level faster, or with fewer resources, and then understand which parts of that improvement came from AI assistance.

The really interesting question is whether AI can help with the bottlenecks that remain as other tasks get cheaper: choosing promising experiments, interpreting surprising results, deciding what to try next. That’s where I’d be looking for evidence of a substantial acceleration, beyond just producing more code.

r001.rationale: It suggests comparing feature delivery time with and without AI, but does not propose randomized trials.

r002.rationale: It does not mention METR or report that AI access slowed task completion.

r003.rationale: It recommends measuring real-world delivery and research progress, but does not discuss cross-checking benchmark evaluations against workplace speedups.
